newsitem.title: JORDAN: Two Jordan banks in country's first bank merger.
newsitem.headline: Two Jordan banks in country's first bank merger.

text.p: Two Jordanian banks, Jordan National Bank and Business Bank, approved on Saturday the first merger in the country's banking history.

The union, prompted by a Central Bank decree for banks to beef up their capital base, creates Jordan's second largest bank in terms of capitalisation and will help it expand its project financing and investment banking arms and widen foreign operations, bankers said.
The new bank retains the name Jordan National Bank, the larger of the two merged banks. Its 42 million dinar ($59.3 million) capital puts it second only to Arab Bank's 44 million dinars.
Shareholders from the two banks on Saturday approved recommendations from a committee which finalised evaluation of assets, shareholders rights and stock evaluations.

Newly appointed board chairman Rajai Muasher told Reuters the merger gave Jordan National Bank room to expand its long-term project finance and launch into new investment banking areas, including mutual funds and corporate bonds that are non-existent in Jordan.
"This allows us to work in wider areas, finance projects on a wider scale and enhances our ability to enter into large-scale project financing in Jordan and the region," he said.
Muasher said the merger would allow Jordan National Bank, which has five branches in Palestinian self-rule areas, four in Lebanon and one in Cyprus, to expand its foreign presence.
The two banks' boards agreed to a merger last June. Cross ownership of more than seven percent between their shareholders has aided the voluntary merger.

The Central Bank, which has been encouraging Jordan's private banks to merge to create stronger banking units in what it views as a crowded market, slashed reserve requirements for merged banks to five percent from 14 percent.
In another move to prod smaller banks into action, it ruled in 1994 that banks must have a capitalisation of at least 20 million dinars. The deadline is the end of 1997.

Before Saturday's merger, Jordan National Bank had capital of 16 million dinars and Business Bank six million. The combined capital has been boosted to 42 million dinars by a transfer from shareholders equity and reserves, the bank said.
Previous attempts at mergers have been resisted by a family-dominated banking sector wary of losing control in mergers.
Total assets of the new bank are worth 629.8 million dinars, putting it fourth among Jordan's 21 private banks after Arab Bank, Housing Bank and Islamic Bank.
Non-combined assets of Jordan National Bank stood at 461.9 million dinars and Business Bank's at 168.1 million dinars.
The new bank's shareholders rights stand at 67.8 million dinars with total deposits of 448.4 million dinars and 319.5 million dinars of loans.

Under the asset evaluation, existing Jordan National Bank shareholders will own nearly 85 percent of the new merged bank's capital, or 36 million dinars. They will get an extra one and a quarter share for every existing share they hold.
Business Bank shareholders will get one new share for every share in their bank and hold only 15 percent of the combined capital.
Twenty-one percent of the equity in the new bank is held outside Jordan including 13.4 percent by Kuwait Investment Bank and three percent by the Beirut-based Arab Insurance Company.
The main shareholders are the Jordanian Muasher family who own over 40 percent of the bank.
